title: Al-Wakil, the Trustee
hook: the Trustee, to whom affairs are entrusted
tomorrow: a man with nothing reaches a crowded well. what does he do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Haqq, the Truth, and the line: the truth. Falsehood vanishes; the Real stays. Today the week closes, and the waiting begins.

Results in two weeks, the email said. Amira has refreshed her inbox four times since breakfast, and checked the scholarship's website twice, as if it might update itself. The essay is in. The interview is done. Last night she went back downstairs and told her dad the truth: it was medium. He laughed and said medium is fine. Nothing left to do now but wait, and waiting has a weight all its own. So what do you do with it?
screen: `RESULTS IN TWO WEEKS.` → `REFRESH. REFRESH.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH THE WAIT?`

segments.voice: Today's Name is for exactly this: Al-Wakil, the Trustee, the one to whom affairs are handed. Surah At-Talaq: "And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him." But trust here isn't sitting on your hands. A man once asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whether he should tie up his camel and trust, or leave it loose and trust. The answer, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi: tie it, and trust. Amira tied every rope she had. Now the camel is in other hands. Trust here isn't instead of the work. It's what comes after it. Look back over the week and you'll see the ropes. Al-Hakim, wise: a hole in a boat that turned out to be a rescue. Al-Wadud, loving: flashcards before sunrise. Al-Majid, glorious: out loud or under your breath. Al-Ba'ith, he raises: tomatoes after rain. Ash-Shahid, witnessed: an ID under a chair. Al-Haqq, the truth: medium, not great. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight. In Surah Al Imran, people warned of a great force gathered against them answered: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil, Allah is enough for us, and the best Trustee. Two weeks of Names in one breath: Al-Hasib, who is enough, and Al-Wakil, who holds what you've handed over.
screen: `HE WILL SUFFICE HIM.` · `TIE IT, AND TRUST.` · `SIX ROPES, ONE WEEK.` · `ENOUGH, AND THE BEST TRUSTEE.` · then, large: `ENTRUSTED.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up. Name one worry, quietly, and let it sit in your open hands, with its weight. Then tip your hands, just slightly, as if passing it to someone you trust. Notice whether your hands feel any different. Leave them open for the sit.
Al-Wakil. The Trustee, the one you hand your affairs to, once the camel is tied. Name fifty-two, and two weeks of Names are done.
The two weeks' last line: entrusted, the camel tied and the rope let go. Until next week.

howItsDone: Muslims say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil (3:173) in hard moments, and the hadith 'tie it, and trust' (Jami' at-Tirmidhi) is taught to show that trust in Allah comes after doing one's part.

fork.setup: your sister's job interview went well, and now she can't sleep for checking her email. what fits Al-Wakil?
options: 'you tied the camel. hand the result over, and check once a day.'
'trusting God means you should stop hoping for the job.'
'keep refreshing; trust means watching closely for the answer.'
fork.reveal: tie it, and trust: do your part, then hand the rest to al-Wakil. trust doesn't cancel hope, and it doesn't need a refresh button.

original.note: Arabic: the Trustee, the one affairs are handed to. 3:173: ni'mal wakil, the best Trustee.

what it means: the Trustee you hand your affairs to after you've done your part.
what a scholar hears: 65:3 promises He will suffice whoever trusts; Tirmidhi's camel hadith joins effort and trust; 3:173 pairs al-Hasib's 'enough' with ni'mal wakil.

Stop caring about the result. Trust means not wanting it anymore.
chat.meaning: Tie it, and trust: Amira did her part. Al-Wakil holds what's handed over, and trust doesn't require giving up hope.
